      resolved="$dir/$imp"

    if [ -z "${seen[$resolved]}" ]; then
      queue+=("$resolved")

Several of the patterns below are strong signals the server currently doesn't validate. ## Critical — Stored XSS in the leaderboard `js/game/UIManager.js:820-823` and `:689-691` build the leaderboard and "top catcher" panel with raw template-literal `innerHTML`, interpolating `p.name` / `topCatcherName` **unescaped**: ```js html += `${p.name}...` this.highscoreContainer.innerHTML = html; ``` Your own name field is fully client-controlled (`initIdentity()` in `PenguinManager.js:142` just lets `localStorage.penguinName` be anything, and it's broadcast raw in every `updatePenguin` emit). Contrast this with `RemotePenguin.js:80` which correctly uses `nameTag.textContent` — the leaderboard is the one place that skipped escaping. Anyone can set their name to `` and it executes in every other visitor's browser the moment they open the leaderboard/stats panel. This is worse than any point cheat — it's a full client-takeover vector (steal sessions, auto-farm points for the attacker, deface the site for everyone). **Fix: use `textContent` for name segments, or HTML-escape server-side/client-side before interpolating.** ## High — Infinite points (client decides when you "caught" a fish) `PenguinManager.js:864-876`: ```js checkFishCollision(player) { ... if (dist < GameConfig.FISH_COLLISION_RADIUS) { this.network.emitCatchFish(player.id, player.name); } } ``` The distance check runs entirely client-side against the client's own `player.x/y` (which is itself broadcast raw, unvalidated — see below). Nothing stops calling this directly from devtools: ```js setInterval(() => window.penguinManager.network.emitCatchFish(window.penguinManager.myPenguinId, "x"), 10); ``` If the server increments score on any `catchFish` message from a connected id/secret without independently checking "is a fish actually active, and is this penguin's *server-known* position within radius, and has it not already been claimed" — that's unlimited score. Same pattern for `emitCatchPowerUp` (`:878-908`). **Fix: server must own fish/powerup existence, do its own proximity check against server-tracked position, and single-claim each spawn (lock on first valid catch).** ## High — Position is 100% client-authoritative `NetworkManager.js:369-388` broadcasts `x`, `y` straight from client state every 50ms, with no server-side speed/collision sanity check implied anywhere in this code. That enables teleporting anywhere (instant "proximity" to fish/shop/ice holes/duel opponents) and is the root cause that makes finding #2 trivial without even needing real movement. **Fix: server should track authoritative position, clamp per-tick delta to max walk/slide speed, and use *its* copy for any proximity-gated reward.** ## High — Freeze/griefing without proof of a hit `NetworkManager.js:491-500`, `emitFreeze(id, duration, attackerId)`: ```js this.socket.emit('freezePlayer', { id, duration, secret: myPenguinSecret, attackerId, attackerSecret: myPenguinSecret }); ``` `id` (the victim) and `duration` are attacker-chosen, with only the *attacker's own* secret proving identity — there's no server-side check that a snowball actually connected. If the server just believes this, any player can: ```js window.penguinManager.network.emitFreeze("", 999999, window.penguinManager.myPenguinId); ``` to permanently freeze anyone (huge griefing/advantage tool in duels or general play). **Fix: freezing should be a consequence the server derives itself from server-tracked snowball collisions, never a client-issued command with an arbitrary target+duration.** ## Medium — "Infinite health" via client-only shield/giant check There's no HP stat; invulnerability is `powerUpType === 'shield' | 'giant'`, and the check that skips a freeze is done **entirely on the receiving client's own in-memory object** (`NetworkManager.js:165-174`, and again in `PenguinManager.js:1167/1228`): ```js if (localPlayer.powerUpType === 'shield') { localPlayer.powerUpType = null; ... } ``` Since `player.powerUpType` is just a JS property on your own client, you never need to actually buy/catch a shield: ```js window.penguinManager.penguins.find(p=>p.isPlayer).powerUpType = 'giant'; // permanent immunity + 3x collision radius ``` This makes you immune to freezing/collision loss locally forever, no server round-trip needed. **Fix: power-up state and its immunity effect must be server-authoritative and pushed to the client, not read from the client's own broadcast field.** ## Medium — Admin gate is a hardcoded public string `GameConfig.js:94`: `ADMIN_PENGUIN_IDS: ['hqet3ipdt1']`. Your `penguinId` is client-generated (`PenguinManager.js:147-148`, `Math.random().toString(36)`) and stored in `localStorage` with **no server binding to a real account** — first-come-first-served on the id string. Since the admin id is shipped in this public JS file, anyone can do: ```js localStorage.setItem('penguinId', 'hqet3ipdt1'); location.reload(); ``` and (if they're first, or if the real admin hasn't claimed it / the server doesn't lock id ownership) get `isAdmin() === true`, unlocking `teleportTo()`/`listWorlds()` and whatever else keys off `isAdmin()`. The comment at `PenguinManager.js:166-169` already flags this as "not real auth" — good self-awareness, but worth confirming nothing server-side actually trusts this client `isAdmin()` for anything beyond convenience. **Fix: real admin auth needs a server-side secret/credential, never a client-visible id match.** ## Medium — Any client can overwrite server enemy/platform lists `emitRegisterEnemies`/`emitRegisterPlatforms` (`NetworkManager.js:441-489`) fire automatically for **every** client on load and on every world transition (`PenguinManager.js:86-87`, `MapManager.js:370-372`) with fully attacker-controlled contents (fire rate, volley, patrol range, aggressive/persistent flags — or an empty array). If the server just accepts the last writer, a cheater can zero out enemies for a hazard-free world, or crank enemy aggression to grief others. **Fix: this registration should be idempotent/validated against the known map data, not blindly trusted per-client.** ## Low — Live debug backdoor: `test_addItem` `js/penguins.js:107-116` wires `window.addTestItem(type)` straight to a `test_addItem` socket event (`NetworkManager.js:526-532`) with no admin gate at all in the client. If your server still implements this handler in production, it's a free item-grant path discoverable by anyone who reads this public file. **Fix: gate/remove this handler server-side outside of dev/staging.** --- **Bottom line:** the client is doing almost all of the trust-sensitive decision-making — "did I catch this," "am I near that," "am I shielded," "is this player an admin," "what does this world's danger look like" — and just telling the server what happened. The fix pattern is the same everywhere: move each of these checks to be derived from server-tracked state, and treat every client emit as a *request*, not a *fact*. Want me to also pull `page/editor_io.php` and the level-editor JS (referenced from `MapManager.js`'s `fetchServerMapList`/`loadWorldFromServer`) to check that endpoint for injection/path-traversal risk, since it's an HTTP endpoint rather than a socket event?

## Realistic exploitability

The honest answer: **you should not leave these as-is.** Almost every one of these requires nothing more than a visitor pressing F12 and typing one or two lines into the browser console — no proxy tools, no scripting knowledge, no account. That's because `window.penguinManager` and `window.penguinManager.network` are globally exposed, and the code even ships console helpers with comments explaining how to use them (`whoami()`, `addTestItem()`, `teleportTo()`). A curious 12-year-old player opening devtools to see error messages would stumble onto this by accident.

Ranked by how little effort it takes:

| # | Issue | What a player actually does | Skill needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | Infinite points | Paste `setInterval(()=>window.penguinManager.network.emitCatchFish(window.penguinManager.myPenguinId,"x"),10)` into console | **Trivial** — copy/paste one line |
| 8 | Free items | `window.addTestItem('color_rainbow')` — literally documented in the shipped comment | **Trivial** — the code tells you how |
| 5 | Freeze immunity | `window.penguinManager.penguins.find(p=>p.isPlayer).powerUpType='giant'` | **Trivial** — one line |
| 6 | Fake admin | `localStorage.setItem('penguinId','hqet3ipdt1'); location.reload()` — the ID is sitting in plain text in the public JS | **Trivial** — copy the ID out of the source, one line |
| 1 | XSS in leaderboard | Set your name to a script payload, catch one fish so it lands on the leaderboard | **Trivial** — two lines, but now *every other visitor* who opens the leaderboard runs your JS, not just you |
| 3 | Teleport | `window.penguinManager.penguins.find(p=>p.isPlayer).x = 9999` | **Trivial** — one line, mainly useful to make #2/#4 more effective |
| 4 | Freeze-griefing others | Same as above but needs a target's `penguinId`, which is visible in the Network tab (every broadcast includes it) | **Easy** — open Network tab, watch a socket frame, copy an id |
| 7 | Overwrite enemies/platforms | Call `network.emitRegisterEnemies()` with a crafted array | **Easy** — needs reading this code first, but the function is right there on the exposed object |

None of these need reverse engineering, a debugger, or writing real exploit code — the attack surface is "read the JS you already gave everyone, then call the functions it exposes." That's the core problem: gameplay-critical decisions (did I catch this fish, am I shielded, am I an admin, where am I standing) are made by the client and simply reported to the server as fact.

**What I'd actually prioritize:**
- **Fix now:** the leaderboard XSS (#1) — this is a real web vuln that can hit any visitor's browser, not just a game-balance issue, so it carries more risk than "someone gets a high score." Infinite points (#2) and the freeze-griefing command (#4) are next — they directly ruin the game for everyone else.
- **Fix soon:** server-side position tracking (#3) — it's the root enabler for several of the others, so fixing it raises the bar across the board even before you've locked down every individual event.
- **Low urgency, but worth a cleanup pass:** the admin-ID trick (#6) and `test_addItem` (#8) — only genuinely dangerous if `isAdmin()` or that debug path is wired to something more powerful server-side than what I could see from the client. Worth a quick check of your server code, but not an emergency if they only unlock convenience commands today.

None of this requires a rewrite — it's the same fix repeated: move each "did this happen" check (fish caught, near shop, shielded, is admin, hit by snowball) onto the server, and escape the leaderboard HTML. The client can keep predicting/animating locally, it just can't be the one deciding what counts.

That error is just a JS console quirk, not a game bug — `const` persists across separate console entries in the same page session, so redeclaring `player` the second time collides with the first. Two ways around it:

**Just reassign, don't redeclare:**
```js
player.x = 1000; player.y = 100;
```

**Or always use `let` (which permits reassignment safely in the console):**
```js
let player = window.penguinManager.penguins.find(p => p.isPlayer);
player.x = 1000; player.y = 100;
```
(`let` will still complain on a second paste in some consoles — if so just drop the `let player = ...` line on later runs and reuse the variable.)

Your first test did work (the `100` you saw is just the console echoing the `y = 100` assignment). Now check whether it actually **stuck**:

1. **Look at your own penguin on screen** — did it visibly jump to the new spot, or did it snap back within a frame or two? If your movement/physics loop recalculates `x`/`y` from keys+gravity every tick regardless of what you set, walking (pressing a key) will immediately overwrite your manual edit — so test this while standing still.
2. **Check tab B (a second window as another visitor)** — does *their* view of your penguin also jump to x=1000? That tells you whether the server relayed your fabricated position to everyone, or corrected/ignored it.
3. **Try triggering something proximity-gated from the fake position** — e.g. teleport near the shop coordinates (`SHOP_X: 200, SHOP_Y: 81` from `GameConfig.js`) without actually walking there, and see if the shop bubble/interaction becomes available anyway.

If tab B sees you at the fake coordinates and proximity checks fire based on it, that confirms the server has no authoritative position check.

`AntiCheat.js` is well-built for what it does:

It's not reactively sanitizing your input each time; it just never reads that field again once you have a name on record.

So to directly answer: no, there's no way to rename yourself to a custom name — legitimate or malicious — through anything we've found. The name field in `catchFish`/`updatePenguin` payloads is write-once-then-ignored from the server's side, not a live "set your display name" control.

But it's currently *unreachable* in practice, because there's no live path left for a client to get an arbitrary string into the `name` field the server actually stores and broadcasts. It's defused by accident (or by a deliberate "names are server-owned" design), not by an actual sanitization fix.
